name: Amperon: AI forecasting for power demand, renewables and prices
title: Amperon: AI forecasting for power demand, renewables and prices
answer: Amperon is a forecasting company founded in 2018 whose site describes AI-powered demand, renewable generation and price forecasts for utilities, retailers and independent power producers. Its most useful single item is a blog post on integrating ECMWF's AI weather model AIFS into its production pipeline, which argues that AI weather models are trained on numerical reanalysis, still depend on numerical output as an initial condition, and remain weaker than numerical prediction during extreme events. The site also documents three strategic investments and its market expansion.

sections.body: This is the corporate website of Amperon, a forecasting technology company founded in 2018, read across 60 pages on 30 September 2026. The pages in the findings are the company's blog, its newsroom press releases and its resources hub, which indexes blog posts, webinars, accuracy reports, white papers, news, market snapshots, case studies and ebooks on energy forecasting. The material is written by the vendor about its own products, customers and investors, so it is company communication rather than independent research or regulation. The releases carry dates from July 2024 through January 2026, while the blog posts in the findings are undated.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: Amperon publishes blog posts, newsroom releases and a resources hub describing its forecasting products and the methods behind them. The most detailed technical piece explains why the company added ECMWF's AI weather model, AIFS, to a pipeline that already runs numerical weather prediction in production. It traces AI weather from NVIDIA's first model in 2022 through Google DeepMind's GraphCast to ECMWF's AIFS in 2024, and says the leading models were in operational use by 2025. It argues that AI weather is not independent of numerical weather, because every production model is trained on ERA5, which is itself built from numerical models, and most still need numerical output as an initial condition. It notes that numerical prediction still outperforms AI during extreme events, and that a degree of temperature error translates directly into load, price or renewable generation forecast error. The releases describe demand, renewable generation and price forecasts used by retailers, utilities and independent power producers, a launch on Snowflake Marketplace in July 2024 using 15-minute meter data, weather data and historical grid data, a mid-term grid demand forecast reaching seven months ahead, and strategic investments from National Grid Partners in March 2025, Acario in July 2025 and Samsung Ventures in January 2026.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: Amperon says numerical weather prediction has added roughly one day of forecast skill per decade, with resolution tightening from 100km grids in the 1980s to about 10km operationally today, and that AI models compressed roughly seven years of traditional progress into two. It says AI inference runs in minutes on a single GPU or TPU rather than hours on high-performance computing clusters, roughly 100 times cheaper, and that ERA5 carries a roughly two-degree temperature gap from raw observations in many regions. Its March 2025 release reports an average 10% accuracy improvement over the previous six months and expansion into 15 European countries in June 2024, and its January 2026 release says it has active forecasts in 27 countries. National Grid Partners committed $100 million to AI solutions for the energy system. The extreme weather article cites $112.9 billion in damage and 152 deaths from Hurricane Ian, 18 U.S. disasters costing at least $1 billion each in 2022, and 360 disasters since 1980 exceeding $2.57 trillion.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in this industry gets a vendor's account of how AI weather models are actually used in power forecasting, which is the specialist layer that sells accuracy to utilities and energy desks. The AIFS post is the most useful part, because it sets out the dependency of AI weather on numerical reanalysis, the cost advantage at inference, and the remaining weakness during extreme events, which is the risk a trading desk or utility cares about most. The investment releases show utility and gas company venture arms backing this layer, and the product releases show what is being sold, demand, renewable generation and price forecasts, including a mid-term grid demand forecast reaching seven months ahead.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Energy

sections.body: The site is Amperon's own marketing and news output, so accuracy claims such as outperforming incumbents are self-reported and no independent benchmark or methodology is given. The blog posts in the findings carry no dates. The resources hub is an index of further material rather than a document in itself, and the case study listing is truncated. Nothing on the pages read covers pricing, model architecture in detail, or how forecasts perform against named competitors outside the company's own statements. The extreme weather article mixes disaster cost statistics with product promotion.
